newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian liberals face monumental farm reform task.
newsitem.headline: Russian liberals face monumental farm reform task.

text.p: Russia's young liberals face a monumental task in agricultural reform following the sacking of Alexander Zaveryukha, the conservative deputy prime minister who presided over the worst harvests in three decades.

Analysts say Zaveryukha's removal in this week's cabinet reshuffle should give more power to Agriculture Minister Viktor Khlystun, who is trying to raise extra funds for the farm sector this year by securing commercial bank credits.
Under Zaveryukha, who was responsible for agriculture, the sector has been one of the slowest to adapt to market reforms and its output has fallen steeply in recent years.
"The process of reform is moving, albeit slowly," Zaveryukha said earlier this month.

But the slow changes have produced some sobering figures. Imports comprise about 40 percent of Russia's entire food market and Moscow is aiming to stabilise grain output in 1997 with a net harvest of 70 million tonnes.
But the goal is still a far cry from crops of over 100 million tonnes in the 1970s and 1980s under communism.
A drive to privatise farmland faltered under fire from conservatives in the government, many of whom favoured huge, Soviet-era collective farms.
Private farms account for less than five percent of the total, with about 12 million hectares (30 million acres), but their share of output is already above five percent.
Analysts said Khlystun's drive to raise commercial loans will be made difficult by a lack of government guarantees for the credits.

But Khlystun will be bolstered by President Boris Yeltsin's appointment of Nizhny Novgorod regional governor Boris Nemtsov as first deputy prime minister. Yeltsin's reshuffle swept aside conservatives in favour of reformers.
"Nemtsov is likely to support Khlystun because of his experience in Nizhny Novgorod, where Nemtsov carried out land reforms," said Andrei Sizov, President of SovEcon Ltd.

Nizhny Novgorod was home to a model voluntary privatisation project spearheaded by the International Finance Corporation, the private sector arm of the World Bank. So far the experiment has failed to take root across the rest of the country.
Zaveryukha's exit will have little effect on the next harvest, which is heading for the third poor result in a row, analysts said.
Russia produced a net 69.3 million tonnes of grain in 1996, compared with 63.4 million in 1995. Both, achieved during Zaveruykha's tenure, were the worst in three decades.
Zaveryukha seemed more at home working the land than walking the Kremlin corridors of power, the analysts said.
His dismissal came as no shock to farm industry watchers, who said his conservative face would not fit in with Yeltsin's new entourage of fresh-faced reformers.
Whether he will be offered a new, more junior government position is still unclear, but Zaveryukha has suggested he favours the fields of his native Orenburg farmland.
"I do not intend to return to the government," he was quoted by Interfax news agency as saying on Tuesday. "I was never burning with desire to get to Moscow, and now I am off to Orenburg."

Zaveryukha paid lip service to reform but seemed to prefer the earthy odours of the collective farm. Interfax quoted him as saying he wanted to be in Orenburg for the start of spring sowing "to feel the charm of the smell of diesel fuel and hear the sound of tractors working".
He was the conservative farm lobby's man in the cabinet, entrusted by scores of farmers with winning as much cheap cash as possible for growing crops.
But as he ran up against tight state budgets, he could not implement the major structural changes that Russia's bloated, inefficient farm sector sorely needs.

"The government and the Agriculture Ministry worked through Zaveryukha, and his role was really just to mediate and lobby," said Sizov. "He was lobbying for more government money to the farm complex, but he didn't have much success."
